title: Cybersecurity Fundamentals
summary: Learn the CIA triad and common threats, strong authentication, network and device security, vulnerability management, risk analysis and incident response, the foundations of a career in cybersecurity.
audience: IT students, support staff, developers, small-business owners and future security professionals

body.p: Cybersecurity protects systems, networks and data from attack, damage and unauthorised access. Professionals describe the goals with the CIA triad: confidentiality (only authorised people can see data), integrity (data is accurate and not tampered with) and availability (systems work when needed). Every control you add should protect at least one of the three.

list: Phishing: fake emails, SMS or calls that trick people into giving passwords or money; still the most common way in.
Malware: viruses, trojans, spyware and ransomware, which encrypts files and demands payment.
Weak or reused passwords that attackers guess or take from earlier breaches.
Unpatched software with known vulnerabilities.
Misconfiguration, such as a database left open to the internet.
Insider threats: careless or malicious staff.
Denial-of-service attacks that flood a service until it fails.

body.p: Attackers range from opportunistic criminals sending millions of scam messages, to organised groups targeting banks and mobile-money platforms, to state-backed groups. Most attacks are not sophisticated; they exploit basic weaknesses. That is good news, because basic defences stop most of them.

body.tip: Think like a defender: list what you must protect, who might want it, and the easiest way in. Fix the easiest ways first.

body.p: Authentication proves who someone is; authorisation decides what they may do. Strong authentication combines factors: something you know (a password), something you have (a phone or security key) and something you are (a fingerprint). Multi-factor authentication (MFA) blocks most account takeovers even when a password leaks.

The number of possible passwords is the number of possible characters raised to the length. An 8-letter lowercase password has 26⁸, about 2.1 x 10¹¹ possibilities; at 10 billion guesses a second (possible offline against a weakly protected password store) that is about 21 seconds. Using all 95 keyboard characters for 8 characters still takes only about 7.7 days. A 12-character password from 62 letters and digits takes about 10 000 years at the same speed. Long passphrases of several random words are both strong and memorable.

list: Use a password manager to create and store unique passwords for every account.
Turn on MFA, preferring an authenticator app or security key over SMS.
Systems should store passwords only as slow, salted hashes, never in plain text.
Apply least privilege: give each account only the access it needs, and remove access when people leave.

body.tip: Check whether your email appears in known breaches using a reputable breach-notification service, and change any reused passwords.

body.p: Networks connect devices, so they are also how attacks travel. Defence in depth uses several layers so that one failure does not expose everything.

list: Firewalls allow or block traffic by address, port and protocol. Only open the ports a service needs: for example 443 for HTTPS websites; keep remote-access ports such as 22 (SSH) and 3389 (Remote Desktop) closed to the internet or restricted.
Encryption in transit: use HTTPS, secure Wi-Fi (WPA2 or WPA3) and VPNs on untrusted networks.
Network segmentation: keep guest Wi-Fi, staff computers, payment systems and cameras on separate networks.
Endpoint protection: keep operating systems updated, run reputable anti-malware and enable disk encryption.
Change default passwords on routers, cameras and other devices.

body.p: Monitoring completes the picture. Logs from firewalls, servers and applications show what happened; security tools raise alerts on suspicious patterns such as many failed logins from one address.

body.tip: Make an inventory of every device and service you run. You cannot protect what you do not know exists.

body.p: A vulnerability is a weakness that can be exploited, such as a software bug or an insecure setting. Publicly known vulnerabilities receive CVE identifiers and severity scores (CVSS, from 0 to 10). Attackers scan the internet for systems missing patches within days, sometimes hours, of a fix being released.

list: Discover: keep an inventory and scan systems regularly with approved tools.
Prioritise: fix critical, internet-facing and actively exploited issues first.
Remediate: apply patches or configuration changes, or add a temporary workaround.
Verify: rescan to confirm the fix, and record what was done.
Remove software and accounts you do not use.
Follow published hardening guides (benchmarks) for operating systems and cloud services.
Never leave storage buckets or databases publicly open by accident.
For developers: validate input, use parameterised database queries to prevent SQL injection, and keep dependencies updated.

body.tip: Only test systems you own or have written permission to test. Unauthorised scanning or hacking is illegal in most countries, including under cybercrime laws in Nigeria, Kenya and South Africa.

body.p: Security budgets are limited, so organisations manage risk: they estimate how likely each threat is and how much harm it would cause, then reduce the biggest risks first. Options are to reduce the risk with controls, transfer it (for example with insurance), avoid the activity, or accept it knowingly.

One simple method uses annual loss expectancy (ALE). If a server worth R200 000 to the business would lose 25% of its value in an incident (the exposure factor), the single loss expectancy is 200 000 x 0.25 = R50 000. If such an incident is expected once every two years (an annual rate of 0.5), ALE = 50 000 x 0.5 = R25 000 a year. A control costing less than the reduction in ALE is worth considering.

list: Security awareness training helps staff spot phishing and report it quickly, without blame.
Clear policies cover acceptable use, passwords, remote work and data handling.
Data-protection laws (POPIA, the Nigeria Data Protection Act, Kenya's Data Protection Act, GDPR) require appropriate security for personal data and, often, breach notification.
Frameworks such as ISO 27001 and the NIST Cybersecurity Framework organise a security programme.

body.tip: Reward people who report suspicious messages, even false alarms. A culture of reporting catches attacks early.

body.p: No defence is perfect, so prepare to respond. An incident response plan says who does what when something goes wrong, how to contact them, and how decisions are made.

list: Preparation: plans, contacts, tools, training and practice exercises.
Detection and analysis: confirm what happened and how far it spread.
Containment: isolate affected systems, reset compromised accounts, block malicious addresses.
Eradication and recovery: remove the cause, restore clean systems from backups, and monitor closely.
Lessons learned: review what worked and fix the gaps.

body.p: Follow the 3-2-1 rule: keep at least 3 copies of important data, on 2 different types of storage, with 1 copy off-site or offline. Ransomware often tries to encrypt or delete reachable backups, so keep an offline or immutable copy, and test restoring regularly; an untested backup may not work when you need it.
Preserve evidence such as logs during an incident, notify regulators and affected people where the law requires, and communicate honestly with customers.

body.tip: Run a short tabletop exercise: talk through "our files are encrypted, what do we do?" with the team before it happens for real.
